note: Excitation and emission maxima are the values published by the supplier or in the primary literature, for the stated binding state (most nucleic-acid stains shift on binding). dyes.name: DAPI
dyes.target: dsDNA — binds the A–T rich minor groove
dyes.summary: The default nuclear counterstain for fixed cells. Cheap, bright, photostable enough for a counterstain, and it sits in the 405 channel where almost nothing else you want to image lives.
dyes.mwSource: PubChem CID 2954 is the free base (MW 277.32); the dihydrochloride sold for staining is MW 350.25

spectra.note: Values are for DNA-bound DAPI. Free DAPI in water is ~340/488 — the ~27 nm emission blue-shift on binding is what gives the stain its contrast.

stock.storage: −20 °C protected from light, stable ≥ 6 months; a 4 °C working aliquot keeps about a month
stock.note: 1 mg/mL = 2.86 mM. DAPI dissolves slowly — warm to 37 °C and vortex, do not assume it went in.

applications.note: Apply after the secondary antibody, before mounting. Longer than 10 min mostly adds cytoplasmic background.
Bacteria need roughly 10× the mammalian concentration; DAPI crosses the Gram-negative envelope poorly.
Look for punctate extranuclear DNA between the cells.
DAPI is stoichiometric enough for DNA-content histograms in imaging, but PI or DRAQ5 is the better choice on a cytometer.

directions.d: Dilute the 1 mg/mL stock 1:10,000 in PBS — that gives 0.1 µg/mL, which is the ~300 nM every protocol means. The neat draw for one coverslip is far below a pipettable volume, so make an intermediate 1:100 (10 µg/mL) first and take 10 µL of that per mL.
Remove the last antibody wash and add enough DAPI solution to cover the sample. Incubate 5 min at room temperature, in the dark.
Wash 2 × 5 min in PBS. Skipping the washes is the usual cause of a hazy blue background.
Mount in an antifade medium. DAPI signal survives months at 4 °C in a cured mountant.

dyes.hazards: DNA-binding, so treat as a possible mutagen. Gloves, and collect the waste as chemical waste rather than pouring it down the sink.
notes: DAPI is excited well at 355/405 nm but very poorly at 488 nm — if it looks dim on a confocal, check you are not on the wrong line.
It bleeds into the green channel when overstained. If your GFP looks blue-tinged, halve the DAPI.
Hoechst 33342 is the live-cell substitute; DAPI enters intact cells only slowly and unevenly.
The 300 nM / 5 min figure is long-standing convention across published protocols, not a number Thermo states on the D1306 datasheet. Titrate if your background is high.

dyes.name: Hoechst 33342
dyes.target: dsDNA — A–T rich minor groove
dyes.summary: The live-cell nuclear stain. Same channel as DAPI but cell-permeant, so it is what you use when the cells have to stay alive.
dyes.mwSource: PubChem CID 1464 is the free base (MW 452.55); the trihydrochloride trihydrate sold for staining is MW 615.99, confirmed against Thermo Molecular Probes manual MP21486

spectra.note: DNA-bound values. Like DAPI, unbound dye is dimmer and red-shifted.

stock.storage: −20 °C in the dark, ≥ 6 months; protect from light at every step
stock.note: 10 mg/mL = 16.2 mM. Dissolves readily, unlike DAPI.

applications.note: Stain in complete medium, then exchange into fresh medium. No wash step is strictly needed.
Hoechst marks every nucleus, PI only the dead ones. Blue and red channels, no crosstalk.

applications.assay: Cell-cycle / DNA content on live cells
applications.note: Needs longer to equilibrate. Efflux-pump-positive lines under-stain — add verapamil or use 33258 on fixed cells.
Condensed and fragmented nuclei are obvious at 40×.

directions.d: Dilute the 10 mg/mL stock 1:10,000 into pre-warmed complete medium for 1 µg/mL.
Replace the medium with the Hoechst medium and return to the incubator for 10–15 min at 37 °C.
Swap back into fresh pre-warmed medium. Live cells do not tolerate the repeated PBS washes a fixed sample would get.
Image within an hour or two. Hoechst is a DNA binder and 405 nm illumination of a stained live nucleus is genuinely phototoxic — keep the exposure and the laser power down.

dyes.hazards: Binds DNA and is a suspected mutagen. Gloves; chemical waste stream.
notes: 33342 is the cell-permeant one, 33258 is not — the two are otherwise near-identical and are very easy to mix up.
Hoechst + 405 nm is the classic source of unexplained phototoxicity in a time-lapse. If cells stop dividing part-way through a movie, suspect this first.
Cells with active ABC transporters pump Hoechst out — that is the whole basis of the 'side population' assay, and it will also quietly ruin your counterstain.

dyes.summary: A far-red, cell-permeant DNA stain. Its whole reason to exist is that it frees the blue and green channels for everything else.

dyes.target: Nucleic acid (DNA and RNA) — cell-permeant
dyes.summary: The green half of the standard bacterial live/dead pair. It stains every cell in the field; propidium iodide then knocks the signal down in the dead ones.
dyes.mwSource: Proprietary — supplied as a 5 mM DMSO solution (Thermo L7012 component A)

spectra.note: Bound to DNA. Emission shifts slightly on RNA.

stock.storage: −20 °C in the dark, desiccated
stock.note: Sold ready-made at 3.34–5 mM depending on the kit — check your vial, the kits differ.

applications.note: The BacLight ratio. Green = intact membrane, red = compromised. Mix the two dyes 1:1 before adding.
Stains the whole biofilm population; combine with a matrix stain for structure.
Works on cells too small or too dim to see by phase contrast.

directions.d: For live/dead, combine equal volumes of the SYTO 9 and PI stocks first, then dilute the mix 3 µL per mL of bacterial suspension.
Wash the cells into 0.85% NaCl. Rich medium quenches and raises the background badly.
15 min at room temperature, in the dark. Longer does not help and lets PI creep into live cells.
Trap 5 µL under a coverslip, or use an agarose pad. Image within 30 min — the ratio drifts after that.

dyes.hazards: Nucleic-acid binder in DMSO — nitrile gloves, chemical waste.

SYTO 9 also stains extracellular DNA, which will inflate the 'live' signal in a biofilm.
Rich medium is the single most common cause of a useless BacLight result — wash into saline.

dyes.target: DNA (green) and RNA / acidic compartments (red)
dyes.summary: A metachromatic stain: green on double-stranded DNA, orange-red on single-stranded RNA and inside acidic vesicles. Cheap and informative, but the two signals are easy to over-interpret.

Green nucleus, red-orange nucleolus and cytoplasm.

Incubate 5–15 min in the dark at room temperature.
Wash 2 × in PBS. Acridine orange stains everything it touches, including the bench.
Excite at 488 nm and collect green (500–540 nm) and red (>600 nm) simultaneously — the ratio is the readout.

dyes.hazards: Mutagenic frameshift agent (it is a standard Ames-test positive control). Gloves, and keep it off skin — it stains.
notes: The red:green ratio depends on dye concentration as much as on the sample. Fix the concentration and the timing before comparing conditions.
It photoconverts under strong 488 nm light; take the image you care about first.

dyes.name: Ethidium bromide
dyes.target: dsDNA — intercalates between base pairs
dyes.summary: The traditional gel stain, and occasionally a nuclear stain. Included here mainly so its spectra sit alongside the safer alternatives you should probably use instead.
dyes.mwSource: PubChem CID 14710 — ethidium bromide, MW 394.29

spectra.note: DNA-bound. There is a second excitation peak near 300 nm — that is what a UV transilluminator uses. Fluorescence rises ~20-fold on intercalation.

stock.storage: 4 °C in the dark, indefinitely; wrap in foil
stock.note: 10 mg/mL = 25.4 mM. Buy it as a ready-made solution — weighing the powder is the highest-exposure step and there is no reason to do it.

working.range: 0.2–0.5 µg/mL in a gel or staining bath

applications.note: Add after the gel has cooled below ~60 °C. See the Agarose gel electrophoresis protocol.
Gives cleaner, more even bands than in-gel staining, at the cost of a step.

directions.d: SYBR Safe or GelRed give comparable sensitivity with far lower mutagenic hazard. Use EtBr only where a protocol genuinely requires it.
Dilute the 10 mg/mL stock 1:20,000 for 0.5 µg/mL — 5 µL into 100 mL.
Either add to the molten gel below 60 °C, or post-stain the run gel for 20–30 min with gentle rocking.
Rinse 10 min in water to drop the background, then image on a 302 nm transilluminator.
All EtBr waste — gels, buffer, tips, gloves — goes to the designated solid or liquid EtBr waste stream. Never to the sink.

dyes.hazards: Potent mutagen and intercalating agent. Double gloves, a dedicated bench area, and a dedicated waste stream. UV illumination is a skin and eye hazard in its own right — use the shield.
notes: A 302 nm transilluminator damages DNA quickly. If the band is going into a ligation, use a blue-light box and a safer stain.
The classic 'ethidium bromide sensitivity' figure is ~1–5 ng per band; SYBR-family stains beat that.

Add to the gel below 60 °C, or post-stain the run gel 20–30 min with gentle rocking.
Use a blue-light transilluminator (470–500 nm), not UV — it is both brighter for this dye and kinder to the DNA.

dyes.target: dsDNA — bis-intercalating cyanine dimer

spectra.note: DNA-bound. Fluorescence rises 20–30 fold on binding, and emission is broad — it bleeds into the far-red channel.

stock.storage: 4 °C in the dark, ~1 year; do not freeze
stock.note: 1 mg/mL = 1.5 mM. Sold ready-made at 1 mg/mL — buy it that way, the powder is nasty to weigh.

Unbound PI is dim. Wash only if the background is genuinely a problem.

dyes.name: Haematoxylin (Harris)
dyes.target: Nuclei — the aluminium–haematein lake binds DNA-associated phosphate groups

stock.solvent: supplied or made as a working solution — it is not a concentrate
stock.storage: room temperature, months; it oxidises and throws a metallic surface scum — filter before each use
stock.note: Harris's formulation uses mercuric oxide as the oxidant in the original recipe; buy a mercury-free version.

applications.note: Follow with differentiation in acid alcohol and bluing in Scott's tap water substitute. See the H&E protocol.
Much shorter than for H&E — you want a faint counterstain, not competition with the DAB.

directions.d: Haematoxylin oxidises in the bottle and forms a metallic scum on the surface. Filter before every use or that scum ends up on your section.
Immerse 3–5 min. The section will look far too dark — that is expected.
Rinse in running tap water.
Dip in 1% acid alcohol for 2–5 seconds. This is the step that makes or breaks the stain; over-differentiate and the nuclei go pale.
Rinse, then blue in Scott's tap water substitute for 1 min until the nuclei turn from red-purple to crisp blue. Alkaline pH is what converts the colour.
Rinse in water and go straight into the eosin step.

notes: Progressive versions (Mayer's) do not need differentiation and are more forgiving; regressive versions (Harris's) give crisper nuclei if you get the timing right.
The 'bluing' step is a pH change, not another stain. Tap water works in hard-water regions; Scott's substitute works everywhere.

dyes.name: Malachite green
dyes.target: Bacterial endospores — driven into the spore coat by steaming
dyes.summary: The primary stain in the Schaeffer–Fulton endospore procedure. It only penetrates the spore coat with heat, which is exactly what makes the stain specific.
dyes.mwSource: Malachite green chloride, MW 364.91 (supplier certificate of analysis)

stock.storage: room temperature, ≥ 1 year
stock.note: 5% aqueous is the Schaeffer–Fulton working strength.

applications.note: Spores go green, vegetative cells are counterstained pink with safranin. See the endospore protocol.

applications.assay: Spore counting in a sporulating culture
applications.note: Gives an unambiguous spore-to-cell ratio that phase contrast alone can be equivocal about.

directions.d: Air-dry and heat-fix.
Cover the smear with a strip of blotting paper, flood with 5% malachite green, and steam over a boiling water bath for 5 min. Keep it wet — add more stain as it evaporates or the slide will bake.
Let the slide cool, then rinse under running water for 30 s. This removes the dye from vegetative cells but not from spores.
Flood with 0.5% safranin for 30 s, rinse and blot.
Oil immersion. Green spores, pink vegetative cells.

dyes.hazards: Malachite green is toxic and a suspected carcinogen and mutagen. Gloves, and steam it in a fume hood if you have one. The steaming step is a scald hazard.
notes: Without the heat the dye does not enter the spore and the stain simply fails. Letting the slide dry out during steaming is the other classic failure.
Malachite green is also used as an antifungal in aquaculture, which is why it is a regulated residue in fish.

working.time: 5 min with steaming (Ziehl–Neelsen) or 5 min cold (Kinyoun's)
working.temp: steam, or room temperature for Kinyoun's
working.wash: rinse, then decolourise in acid alcohol

applications.note: Acid-fast bacilli stay red after acid-alcohol; everything else is counterstained blue with methylene blue.
Higher phenol replaces the heat. Easier and safer, slightly less sensitive.
The weaker acid preserves the staining of partially acid-fast organisms.

directions.d: Air-dry and heat-fix. Handle any suspected mycobacterial specimen in a Class II cabinet.
Flood with carbol fuchsin and steam for 5 min, keeping it wet. Or use Kinyoun's cold formulation and leave it 5 min without heat.
Rinse with water.
Apply 3% acid alcohol until the runoff is nearly colourless — usually 1–2 min. This is the discriminating step.
Flood with methylene blue for 1 min, rinse and blot.
Oil immersion at 100×. Red bacilli against a blue background.

dyes.hazards: Phenol is corrosive, readily absorbed through skin, and toxic. Basic fuchsin is a suspected carcinogen. Fume hood, gloves, eye protection. Clinical specimens suspected of containing M. tuberculosis are a serious infection risk and must be handled in a Class II cabinet under BSL-3 practice.
notes: Acid-fastness comes from the mycolic acid wall, not from the dye. A poorly grown or damaged mycobacterium can lose it.
Auramine-rhodamine fluorescence microscopy has largely replaced Ziehl–Neelsen in clinical labs because it is far faster to screen.

dyes.name: Toluidine blue O
dyes.target: Acidic tissue components — metachromatic on sulfated glycosaminoglycans
dyes.summary: A metachromatic stain: it goes blue on most tissue but shifts to red-purple on sulfated proteoglycans, which makes mast cell granules and cartilage matrix jump out.
dyes.mwSource: Toluidine blue O chloride, MW 305.83 (supplier certificate of analysis)

stock.storage: room temperature, ≥ 1 year
stock.note: 1% aqueous, often buffered to pH 2.5 for metachromasia.

applications.note: The standard stain for orienting a semi-thin section before cutting ultrathins for EM.
Metachromatic red-purple granules against a blue background.
Lignified walls go blue-green, pectin-rich walls pink.

directions.d: Flood the section with the working solution for 30 s – 5 min depending on the application. Semi-thin resin sections need heat: 30 s on a 60 °C hotplate.
Rinse in water and blot. Toluidine blue over-stains easily — start short.
Brightfield. Look for the colour shift, not just intensity — the metachromasia is the information.

dyes.hazards: Low hazard. Stains skin and fabric.
notes: The metachromatic shift is pH-dependent — buffer to pH 2.5 if the red-purple colour is the point.
It is the fastest way to check a resin block before committing to ultrathin sectioning.

dyes.name: Nigrosin
dyes.target: Nothing — it stains the background, leaving cells and capsules clear
dyes.summary: A negative stain. It does not stain the cells at all — it darkens the background so the unstained cells stand out as bright shapes, which means no heat fixation and no shrinkage.

stock.storage: room temperature, indefinitely; filter or autoclave to keep it sterile
stock.note: 10% aqueous nigrosin is the standard negative-stain reagent.

applications.note: The capsule excludes both the nigrosin and any counterstain, so it appears as a clear halo. Heat would collapse it, which is why negative staining is the only reliable capsule method.
No fixation means no distortion — the cells keep their true shape.
Unshrunken cells give an honest size measurement.

directions.d: Place a small drop of nigrosin at one end of a clean slide and mix in a loopful of culture. Do not heat-fix at any point.
Bring a second slide up against the drop at about 30°, let the drop spread along the edge, then push it smoothly along the first slide to draw a thin film — exactly like a blood smear.
Let it air-dry completely. No heat, no rinse.
Oil immersion at 100×. Cells appear as bright refractile shapes on a dark grey background; a capsule shows as a clear halo around the cell.

dyes.hazards: Low hazard. Nigrosin is a dye mixture rather than a defined compound; treat as an irritant. It stains everything it touches.
notes: Heat fixation destroys capsules — that is why this is a negative stain. If you can see a halo you have done it right.
India ink is used identically and is the traditional choice for Cryptococcus in CSF.
A too-thick smear is the usual failure. The film should be a barely visible grey wash, not a black stripe.

dyes.name: India ink
dyes.target: Nothing — a particulate background stain excluded by capsules
dyes.summary: The other negative stain. A suspension of carbon particles too large to enter a capsule, so capsules show up as clear halos. The classic rapid test for Cryptococcus neoformans in cerebrospinal fluid.

stock.storage: room temperature; filter or centrifuge before use to remove clumps
stock.note: Not all inks work — some modern inks contain shellac or biocides. Use a stated microbiological grade or Pelikan drawing ink.

applications.note: A wide clear halo around a budding yeast is the classic finding. Sensitivity is only around 50% — a negative does not exclude cryptococcal meningitis, and antigen testing has largely superseded it.
Interchangeable with nigrosin.

directions.d: Place a small drop of ink on a slide and mix in an equal volume of the specimen or a loopful of culture.
Lower a coverslip gently to avoid bubbles. This is a wet mount, not a dried smear.
Brightfield or phase contrast at 40×, then oil at 100×. Look for clear halos around the cells.

dyes.hazards: Clinical CSF is a genuine infection risk — handle it in a Class II cabinet under the appropriate containment level. The ink itself is low hazard.
notes: Ink varies wildly between brands; some contain preservatives that lyse cells. Test any new bottle against a known capsulated strain.
Talc and leukocytes are routinely mistaken for capsulated yeast. Look for a budding yeast inside the halo before calling it positive.

dyes.name: Uranyl acetate
dyes.target: The background around the specimen — heavy-metal salts scatter electrons, the specimen does not
dyes.summary: The standard negative stain for phage and virus particles. Fine grain, high contrast, and it fixes the specimen as it stains.
dyes.mwSource: PubChem CID 21226249 is the anhydrous salt (MW 388.12); the dihydrate used for staining is MW 424.15
cubes: Transmission electron microscope — not a light-microscopy reagent

stock.solvent: deionized water — it will not dissolve above about 2%
stock.storage: 4 °C in a dark bottle, ~6 months; discard when it goes cloudy or throws a precipitate
stock.note: 2% (w/v), filtered through 0.22 µm. It is light-sensitive and photoreduces — keep it wrapped.

applications.note: The standard method for imaging phage morphology — head diameter, tail length and the presence of a contractile sheath, which is what family assignment rests on.
Resolves surface detail down to a few nanometres.
Followed by lead citrate for the classic double-stain contrast.

directions.d: Glow-discharge a carbon-coated grid to make it hydrophilic. Without this the sample beads up and you get nothing.

Float the grid on, or pipette 5–10 µL onto, the carbon side and leave 1–2 min. A phage sample should be around 10⁹–10¹⁰ PFU/mL — too dilute and you will find nothing, too concentrated and the particles pile up.
Touch the grid to two drops of deionized water to remove salt and buffer. Salt crystallises and ruins the field.
Touch to a drop of 2% uranyl acetate for 30 s.
Blot the edge on filter paper — do not wipe the surface — and air-dry completely before loading.

dyes.hazards: Uranyl acetate is BOTH radioactive (depleted uranium) AND chemically toxic as a heavy metal, and it is subject to regulatory control in many countries. Use it only under your institution's radioisotope authorisation, in a designated area, with gloves, and dispose of it through the designated radioactive-waste stream. Never handle the powder outside a controlled area.
notes: Uranyl formate gives finer grain for higher-resolution work but is much less stable — it must be made fresh.
Where regulation makes uranyl salts impractical, ammonium molybdate and phosphotungstate are the usual substitutes at some cost in contrast.
It photoreduces under light, which is why the bottle is wrapped and why an old solution stains poorly.

dyes.name: Uranyl formate
dyes.target: The background around the specimen — heavy-metal salts scatter electrons, the specimen does not
dyes.summary: A finer-grained uranyl stain used where resolution matters — single-particle EM and structural work. It must be made fresh every time.
cubes: Transmission electron microscope — not a light-microscopy reagent

stock.solvent: boiling deionized water, then cooled and filtered
stock.storage: MAKE FRESH — it is usable for a few hours at most and degrades visibly
stock.note: 0.75% (w/v). Dissolve in boiling water, cool, adjust to pH ~4.5 with 5 M NaOH, and filter through 0.22 µm immediately before use.

working.buffer: the stain itself, at pH 4.5, adjusted with NaOH

applications.note: Finer grain than uranyl acetate, so it supports higher-resolution reconstructions.
The standard first look at a complex before committing to cryo-EM.

directions.d: Dissolve to 0.75% in boiling deionized water, cool, adjust to pH 4.5 with 5 M NaOH, and filter through 0.22 µm. Use it within a few hours.
Glow-discharge the grid, apply the sample, and leave 1 min.
Wash on two drops of water, then stain on two successive drops of uranyl formate — 5 s then 30 s.
Blot at the edge and dry completely.

dyes.hazards: Radioactive and chemically toxic heavy metal, under the same regulatory controls as uranyl acetate. Designated area, radioactive-waste stream, institutional authorisation required.
notes: The instability is the trade-off for the grain size — a solution more than a few hours old gives visibly worse images.
The two-drop staining sequence is standard practice and does measurably improve the result over a single drop.

dyes.name: Phosphotungstate (PTA)
dyes.target: The background around the specimen — heavy-metal salts scatter electrons, the specimen does not
dyes.summary: A negative stain that works at neutral pH, which makes it the right choice for specimens that fall apart in the acid conditions uranyl salts need.
cubes: Transmission electron microscope — not a light-microscopy reagent

stock.solvent: deionized water, adjusted to pH 7.0 with NaOH
stock.storage: room temperature, ~1 year; it is stable, unlike the uranyl stains
stock.note: 2% (w/v). Phosphotungstic acid is strongly acidic as supplied — neutralise it before use or it will destroy the specimen.

working.buffer: the stain itself, at pH 7.0, adjusted with NaOH

applications.note: Use for acid-labile specimens — many enveloped viruses and some phages lose their tails at pH 4.
Neutral pH preserves these delicate appendages far better than uranyl acetate.

directions.d: Adjust the 2% solution to pH 7.0 with NaOH. This is essential — the acid as supplied is around pH 1.5.
Glow-discharge the grid and apply the sample for 1–2 min.
Touch to two drops of water.
Touch to a drop of 2% PTA pH 7.0 for 30 s.
Blot at the edge, air-dry completely.

dyes.hazards: Phosphotungstic acid is corrosive as supplied and harmful if swallowed or inhaled. Gloves, eye protection, and neutralise before use. Not radioactive — which is precisely why many labs prefer it.
notes: Coarser grain than uranyl acetate, so contrast and resolution are both lower. The trade is specimen preservation.
It penetrates some specimens rather than staying outside them, giving a positive rather than a negative image — check what you are actually looking at.

dyes.name: Ammonium molybdate
dyes.target: The background around the specimen — heavy-metal salts scatter electrons, the specimen does not
dyes.summary: A gentle, neutral-pH negative stain. The lowest-contrast of the common options, but also the least damaging — the choice for fragile specimens.
cubes: Transmission electron microscope — not a light-microscopy reagent

stock.storage: 4 °C, several months
stock.note: 1–2% (w/v). Some protocols add 0.1% trehalose to reduce flattening.

working.buffer: the stain itself, at pH 7.0, adjusted with NaOH or ammonia

applications.note: The mildest of the common negative stains.
Less likely to trigger sheath contraction than an acidic stain — a real problem when you are trying to score native morphology.

directions.d: Bring the 2% solution to pH 7.0.
Glow-discharge the grid and apply the sample for 1–2 min.
Wash on two drops of water, then stain on 2% ammonium molybdate for 30 s.
Blot at the edge and dry.

dyes.hazards: Harmful if swallowed; molybdate is an irritant. Gloves and eye protection. Not radioactive.
notes: Lower contrast than uranyl acetate or PTA — expect to work harder at the microscope.
Adding trehalose or glucose reduces the flattening artefact on soft specimens.
